report:
**Conclusion:** Your view is well supported. Capsaicin is **not an established treatment for breast cancer in humans**, and current evidence does not show that eating chili peppers, taking capsaicin supplements, or using capsaicin products treats a breast tumor.

The positive breast-cancer findings commonly cited are *preclinical*: for example, capsaicin reduced viability and migration and caused cell-cycle arrest in the MDA-MB-231 breast-cancer **cell line**—an experiment in cultured cells, not patients.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33173974/

A scientific review concludes that the clinical value of oral capsaicin as a complement to chemotherapy remains **speculative**. Laboratory and animal effects cannot establish a safe, effective human dose, tumor response, survival benefit, or compatibility with standard breast-cancer therapies.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/

The clinical-trial search result involving capsaicin and breast-cancer patients concerns **neuropathic pain after breast surgery**, rather than treating cancer itself. That distinction matters: topical capsaicin may have a pain-management role, but it is not evidence of anticancer efficacy.  
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03794388

Therefore, capsaicin should not replace evidence-based breast-cancer care (such as surgery, radiation, endocrine therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, or immunotherapy when indicated). Patients considering concentrated capsaicin supplements should discuss them with their oncology team, particularly during active treatment.
